title: How to Build an Office FitOut Budget: Scope, Allowances and Quote Checks
excerpt: A useful FitOut budget explains what is included, what remains uncertain and who supplies each input. Use this guide to prepare a comparable scope for your workplace project.
author: Joe Kelley
metaTitle: Office FitOut Budget Planning Guide Australia | YOS
metaDescription: Build an office FitOut budget with clear scope, allowances, exclusions and decision owners. Compare project-specific proposals before committing to works.
body:
## How do you build a useful office FitOut budget?

Define the workplace brief, inspect the actual premises and identify what is included before comparing totals. A useful budget records the scope, assumptions, allowances, exclusions and inputs still required from consultants, contractors and suppliers.

This guide explains a budgeting method for an Australian workplace project. It does not provide verified market rates, a construction quote or a completed-project cost benchmark. For a local brief, use the [Newcastle office FitOut scope guide](/blog/commercial-fitout-cost-newcastle-2026) alongside site-specific advice.

## Start with the business and the building

Record the intended activities, peak attendance, meeting needs, storage, visitor access and target operating date. Identify existing furniture and building elements you hope to retain, then ask the relevant project team members to assess their suitability.

The site condition, proposed use, landlord requirements, access arrangements and applicable approvals need to be considered for the actual project. Do not assume a fitted office can be reused unchanged or that two properties of the same area need the same work.

**Helpful tip:** separate essential business requirements from preferences before discussing finishes. That gives later scope choices a clear reference point.

## Split the budget into visible workstreams

| Workstream | What to record | Input to clarify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Professional and management inputs | Briefing, design, surveys, consultants and client-side coordination | Scope, deliverables and responsibility for each appointment |
| Existing condition | Retained items, removal, repairs and landlord-provided works | What has been inspected and what is assumed |
| Building works | Quantities, materials, finishes and installation | Drawing revision, inclusions and exclusions |
| Building services | Mechanical, electrical, fire and hydraulic interfaces | Specialist assessment and coordination responsibilities |
| Technology | Network, access control, meeting-room AV and changeovers | Client IT and supplier workstreams |
| Furniture | Product specifications, quantities and retained items | Delivery, assembly, installation and lead times |
| Transition | Moving, staging, disruption and existing-lease exit work | What must happen before the business can operate |
| Allowances and cash flow | Unresolved scope, contingency, GST basis and payment milestones | Who approves changes and when funds are needed |

Keep furniture-only planning separate from a building-works budget. The [office furniture budget guide](/blog/office-furniture-budget-newcastle) helps prepare product and installed-scope inputs.

## Compare proposals on the same basis

Ask each provider to identify the scope revision, quantities, allowances, exclusions, validity period and programme assumptions. Record whether GST is included and which activities sit with the client or another provider.

A lower total may reflect a different scope rather than a lower cost for the same work. List unresolved items in a clarification register and ask for an explanation before treating proposals as comparable.

**Helpful tip:** give every clarification an owner and a date. Record the answer in the budget assumptions so it does not disappear between conversations.

## Test allowances without presenting them as quotes

An allowance is a working input for a defined uncertainty. Record its basis and the step needed to replace it with a project-specific estimate or quote. Keep contingency visible and agree who can authorise its use.

The [FitOut estimator](/resources/fitout-estimator) can help frame an indicative conversation. Check its stated scope and assumptions, then seek the actual site and supplier inputs needed for the business decision. It is not a fixed-price offer or a verified market quotation.

## Connect budget decisions with programme and handover

Confirm supplier-specific lead times rather than assuming a universal furniture or construction timeframe. Landlord inputs, design approvals, access limits, staging and IT changeovers can affect the sequence of decisions.

Before approving a proposal, ask how changes will be documented and how responsibilities for defects, documentation and operating readiness will be tracked.

[Use the office FitOut handover checklist](/blog/office-fitout-handover-checklist)

## What YOS coordinates

YOS acts as the client's project manager, connecting the agreed brief, budget, consultant inputs, appointed contractors, decisions and handover. YOS is not the builder or head contractor; appointed contractors and advisers retain responsibility for their respective work.

[Explore office FitOut project management](/office-fitout) to understand the service, or [send your FitOut project brief](/office-fitout#fitout-enquiry) with the site, project stage and timing you know.

If you are still comparing leased premises, explore [tenant representation](/tenant-rep) so property and workplace requirements can be considered together. You can also [ask a project question](#blog-contact-form) using the form below.
